Recent research cautions against equating strong SASRec accuracy with complex sequence understanding. RecSys 2024’s [Does It Look Sequential?](https://github.com/Antondfger/Does-It-Look-Sequential) evaluates shuffled histories using HR@10, NDCG@10 and recommendation overlap, distinguishing inference perturbations from training on shuffled data. A [2026 benchmark study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) finds simple recency-weighted pairwise models competitive with or superior to reproduced SASRec/eSASRec on several datasets. Recency and item associations can therefore explain performance without higher-order sequence modeling.

[Robust Training of Sequential Recommender Systems with Missing Input Data](https://iris.uniroma1.it/bitstream/11573/1740238/1/Siciliano_Robust-Training_2024.pdf) measures ranking sensitivity after deleting history items; removing the latest interaction particularly disrupts SASRec recommendations. [CoDeR (AAAI 2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/download/33379/35534) distinguishes genuine demand shifts from noisy shifts through counterfactual demand reasoning. Its causal interpretation depends on modeling assumptions; history perturbations alone establish model sensitivity, not actual user intent changes.

Suggested diagnostic synthesis: freeze the trained model and validation candidates; compare recent-item deletion, equal-count random deletion, older-item deletion, and order shuffling that preserves the final item. Separately shuffle the recent window to test local order. Report paired changes in HR@10, target rank and top-10 overlap, with uncertainty across users and repeated random controls. Test repeated interests through item identity or title/description similarity, explicitly labeling semantic similarity as a proxy. Control sequence length, padding and position shifts. Greater disruption from recent-interest removal than matched controls supports reliance on recent evidence; sensitivity without improved validation accuracy can instead indicate brittleness. These are proposed probes, not measured findings for the four Amazon datasets.
